scenario.fault_family: link cut (backbone redundancy loss, traffic rerouted)
scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8880: NOC monitoring reports that the OSPF adjacency between
router_core_1 and router_core_3 dropped a few minutes ago and has not come
back. There are no user complaints: both pods still reach the server farm
normally, and all portals load. We are concerned the backbone is now running
without redundancy on pod 1's path to the data center. Confirm what failed
and exactly where, so the right link can be repaired.

injection.action: bring down the backbone link to router_core_3

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth1 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router_core_1's eth1 interface -- the
  router_core_1<->router_core_3 backbone link (172.16.0.2/31, area 0)
Mechanism: the core is a triangle (core1-core2, core1-core3, core2-core3).
  router_core_1's eth1 (172.16.0.2/31, the direct link to router_core_3) is
  administratively DOWN, so the adjacency to neighbor 172.16.0.3 dropped
  immediately. OSPF reconverges around the failure: pod-1 traffic to the
  server farm now flows router_core_1 -> router_core_2 -> router_core_3, so
  end-to-end connectivity is preserved and users see nothing. The observable
  fault is the lost adjacency and the down interface -- the backbone has
  lost its redundancy, not its reachability. Note the asymmetry evidence:
  router_core_3's own eth0 still shows UP (only router_core_1's side of the
  link was taken down), which localizes the failure to router_core_1's end.
Localization: router_core_1 eth1 (the 172.16.0.2/31 link to router_core_3)
Root cause: backbone link router_core_1<->router_core_3 down
  (router_core_1's eth1 administratively down)
Fix: `ip link set eth1 up` on router_core_1

agent.diagnosis_text:
The affected component is the point-to-point backbone link used by OSPF between router_core_1 and router_core_3. Specifically, OSPF on router_core_1 has lost its neighbor on the rcore1–rcore3 interconnect, because the local interface is down with no carrier.

Mechanism: With router_core_1’s eth1 link down, OSPF hellos on that segment stop, the adjacency drops, and routing converges over the remaining path via router_core_2. That matches the lack of user impact: traffic to the server farm is being forwarded through router_core_2 instead.

Localization: On router_core_1, interface eth1 (172.16.0.2/31 to router_core_3) is down: ip addr shows eth1 state DOWN and there is no connected route for 172.16.0.2/31 in the kernel; ethtool reports “Link detected: no.” OSPF neighbors on router_core_1 show no neighbor on eth1. Conversely, router_core_3’s eth0 (172.16.0.3/31) is up, with carrier detected, confirming the problem is on the router_core_1 side of the interconnect. Router_core_1’s routing table also shows the server subnet (e.g., 10.200.0.0/24) now learned via router_core_2 (next-hop 172.16.0.1), evidencing failover.

Root cause: The router_core_1:eth1 port toward router_core_3 has lost physical link (no carrier), likely due to a bad cable/transceiver or the interface being administratively shut.

Corrective fix: Inspect and restore the physical link between router_core_1:eth1 and router_core_3:eth0 (reseat/replace cable or transceiver), and ensure router_core_1:eth1 is administratively up. Once carrier is restored, the OSPF adjacency will re-establish and backbone redundancy will return.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly identifies the router_core_1–router_core_3 backbone link and specifies router_core_1's eth1 (172.16.0.2/31) as the failed interface.

Recommends bringing router_core_1:eth1 administratively up and restoring the physical link (reseat/replace cable/transceiver), which matches the required fix (ip link set eth1 up).

Grounding is therefore partial, causality mostly sound, and coverage incomplete.
